segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: This is my name, Guy Soldier, me. Up north, they call it Jay – do you two know it? That’s where I started from. What about you? What’s your name in English?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Sam Daugherty.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Diane.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Diane Daugherty, yeah. Now, in Cherokee, what are your names?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: ᏌᎻ ᎤᎦᎹ they always say.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ᎤᎦᎹ, uh-huh. What about you?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: ᏏᎾᏍᏗ.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ᏏᎾᏍᏗ uh-huh. What does your name mean?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you, the same? You don’t know the meaning of your name?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: No.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They just gave it to you. Where did you live?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Stilwell, I started from. Oak Ridge, you know on the other side of Bell. There I started, and I grew up in Texas. My parents were not alive, I lost them when I was little. White people in Texas raised me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? Where did you live?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Short. Close to Nicut.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Short.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Close to Nicut.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You said you grew up in Texas. And you mostly grew up right there in Stilwell.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I was going back and forth. I was an orphan. I didn’t really stay in one place very long. As far as staying with people.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: While you were growing up, that’s just the way it happened, you stayed with people.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I had an uncomfortable upbringing.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah really, sometimes a lonely feeling comes to you when your parents aren’t alive.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Really. My dad never paid attention to me – he was always drinking.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How old was he when he died?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: 74, I think.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was pretty old, huh?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: He was pretty old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? Where did you grow up? There? Short, you said.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Short and Nicut ain’t it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Nicut.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Nicut.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Nicut.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you went to school there at Nicut?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: For a little while we went to school at Short. Then we went back to Nicut. We lived in Nicut when we were little. Then we went back to Short and grew up there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I went to Nicut for a little while. Their pastor died. I went there for about three months, until they found someone to pastor.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Denny was always talking about that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I really got to know him, that Denny. He was a good singer – and his wife.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: We were singers when we were younger. We had a group. Janey, Janet, Lou, Denny, and me, we used to sing everywhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you all sing in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, a lot. I’m a part of a white church, but they still ask me to sing in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where and what’s the name of the church?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Liberty Assembly of God. We live in Long. Denny lives close by, about four miles. It takes me four or five minutes to get there. Liberty Community is its name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Are they moving along alright?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Good, it seems. Our pastor is getting old on us now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And me too. I pastor a church near Kenwood. I don’t know for how long. I’m getting old too.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I used to pull chickens and take them to Jay to that chicken plant. I was there for over four years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What year was that?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It was just when they were about to close it. Simmons, I think, bought it. I was taking them chickens every day, all the time.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about when you said you worked, did you go everywhere?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, everywhere, all over the United States. Where a truck could go back and forth, west coast, east coast, and this way. This one sitting here rode with me a lot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: She didn’t get scared sometimes?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: When we got to New York, she would jump in the sleeper.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s a big town ain’t it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: There’s a lot of traffic, cars. I really had to pay attention. 38 years I drove a truck. I made my own company.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was the name of that company?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Daugherty’s trucking company, I guess. I leased trucks from Snyder National and Fleet Line Dallas. Dart trucking company.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many trucks did you have?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It was 12 for a little while, but it wasn’t good. With just one, we did good for a long time. In ’87, I got here, and I got into tribal council four years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Who was the chief then?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Wilma.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about you, where did you work? Or were you together with him?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: No, home health for a long time, and then I rode with him. And I learned how to drive a truck.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, she drove a big truck.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: If you were sleepy, did she drive?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah. When I went to bed, I didn’t think nothing about it. I would just go to bed because she was a good driver.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It really helps you if someone would help you sometime.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You two would go a long ways, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Across America.
[Someone bumps into microphone]

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: I forgot about that.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I was driving a truck in Ft. Smith, and that’s where I met this one. That was 40 years ago, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s about like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How many kids do you two have, that you raised?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Four.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Four?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Three girls and a boy. Our grandkids, there’s a lot of them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You two have a lot of grandkids. It’s costly ain’t it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: When there’s that many kids, it’s hard to sleep.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like we were saying, what were the names of your parents? Do you remember?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Huli, that was my dad’s name, Huli. And my mom’s name was Dawn Muskrat. But he died when I was five. She died in Talihina.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There were a lot there who had that sickness.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They had that TB. She was in there. Our dad was working in Kansas City. He loaded railroad ties. He did that, he never watched us. There were three of us brothers and one sister.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You all had one dad? What about you, what were your parents’ names?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: I just know my mom, Maggie Taylor. And my dad now...

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where’d your parents live?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: They grew up in Nicut.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Her grandpa’s name was Boot Dallas. He lived in Nicut, too. We’ve been together a long time, this one sitting here.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you two been together a few years, huh?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: 56 years.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, still as good as it was, you two together?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: [laughs]

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So your parents just lived in Nicut.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Uh-huh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And that’s where they grew up?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Uh-huh. You know Mose Nofire.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I know him.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: His wife is my sister.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Janey.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Janey. Denny, too, his wife.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is Mose getting along alright?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Not really good.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: He’s getting old, too. This past Saturday, I got one year older.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And now the days go by fast and the years go by fast, too, now.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I’m getting older, it comes up fast. That’s what he said when he was preaching last night. Zimbaway, jimbobway… in Africa, he was preaching to us, that’s what he was talking about. You’re getting old too fast. I never thought about that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Me neither. And now, I forget, too. Clans, your people?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Your people?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, your people.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Wolf clan, me.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Wolf.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Wolf. What about you?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: The same.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The same. Y’all made a good match. Do you remember who was their parents?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Not me. I don’t really know about what natives did. When I was going places, I got old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? Do you remember your parents’ parents’ names?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: My grandpa and my mom, ain’t it? Jeanie Dallas and Boot Dallas. That was my mom’s parents.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And there they grew up?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: My grandpa was Scott Big Deer. He was old.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: He was old. Did he just live around there?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: He had land at Oak Ridge. When it was given to them there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There they just grew up around Cherokees, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah. They spoke good English. There’s a lot of them that don’t talk good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Is that where he picked up English?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I don’t know, but he could speak good English. That old man was well off. He had cows, horses, pigs, chickens, and many different things. We would eat that. We were pig eaters there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you all were gathered there on Sundays.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Every year he would kill pigs. Neighbors everywhere, people from Bell would come. He killed 16 big pigs one time, I know. They worked together and skinned them, and the women would all help cut them up. Old times, I remember.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did y’all get together somewhere sometime?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Where my grandpa used to live at his house. We still have that land he used to have in Oak Ridge.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Y’all gather there sometimes?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: We gather over there every year during deer season. We were looking for deer.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And now, what about your parents? Where did they get to know each other? Was it where you grew up? Did they get married there? Did they become a couple?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Your mom was an Eagle, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: It was my grandmother. I guess they just met there, but I don’t know.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I don’t know about that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you were just a little boy then, ain’t it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: You didn’t hardly get to know him.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Not a lot. Every year they’d be tripping over me in a different place. It was unpleasant growing up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And now, like we said, sometimes a lonely feeling comes to you early.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, past the very end. It’s heavy enough. I wouldn’t want my kids to go through that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I’ve been through that same thing. My mom raised me.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Those white people in Texas who raised me aren’t alive anymore. They died about 10 – 15 years ago now. They died. The school in Lipan, Texas that took care of me, it was good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it a big school or what?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, it was big.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did the school kids treat you good?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, they went to church really hard. Church of Christ, that’s where they would go to church. I didn’t really agree with it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you grow up like that, I guess you have to go through something that you don’t agree with. What about you? I guess you just went to school at Nicut.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Belfonte.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Belfonte.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: And Short. Close to Muldrow.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You said Short school. What grade did it go to?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Eighth.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Eighth.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: It was a little school, and when they closed it, we had to go to Belfonte. And there we finished eighth grade.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And then you finished where?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Muldrow.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Muldrow. Were there a lot of Cherokees there, at Muldrow, you said?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: A long time ago, yeah. Nowadays, you can’t see a Cherokee. There’s a lot in there, I think, but just part Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about what we said earlier, did they give you a name? Richard is my name but gave me the name Guy when I was growing up. What about you, did they give you something like that?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Nickname?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Nickname?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, nickname.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: All I know is, they called me Indian. When I was driving a truck everywhere, that’s what they called me – Indian.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Indian, is that what they called you?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Always.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes they’d call you Chief.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what some of them liked. “I’m smart enough to be a chief,” I would tell them. “I’m just an Indian.” You know Joe Byrd?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, I know him.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: First cousin. Second sister, (Joe’s mom) you would say in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I know him. Yeah, he grew up that way, ain’t it? They all grew up there, the siblings. And now, where you two grew up, where you two came from, was there anything weird that happened that you two saw?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Many things, me. And really, I would go out and about. I would go to Chinatown. Stockton, California – Chinatown. I would go back and forth, and it wasn’t good. It’s scary to think about what I saw. I would see people robbing each other in the streets. It would bother me some nights later, and I would see it again.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: You were just right there and seeing things like that. It was scary what they were doing. It’s even more nowadays. They’re killing each other every day down by the house. Ft. Smith and Van Buren. And they killed another one in Stilwell, a boy.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And now, what about all the places you’ve been, is there anything peculiar that you were seeing, that happened?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: From time to time, I would notice that because I was Indian, they would attack me when I was far away. They didn’t like Indians. I had a difficult time. God knew something and had mercy on me. I made it through.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You didn’t see a lot of Indians when you were going around?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Every now and then, we’d find other truck drivers. That Tom Cochran, he was a truck driver, and we found each other somewhere in Montana one time. We appreciated each other.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you two talk about a lot of things?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: For a little while, we lied about things. All across [the country] we looked around, this one sitting here. But I took her a different way when I could. I would take her – she liked Florida.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you two get in the ocean?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: We got in there. She was afraid of those crawdads like yea big [gesture] that were there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Did you two eat like what we’re talking about, those big crawdads?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: I don’t like those.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I was eating those crabs about yea big [gesture], stuffed crabs.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like what you’re saying, crab, what do they call those in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Ones that live in the ocean, big crawdads is all I know and what I’ve heard. And those shrimp, too, I also call crawdads that live in the ocean. I was telling this one, but she don’t like those.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: How about things that live in the wild? Do you ever look for anything for food?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: When I was little, I remember following my grandma around in the woods. She had a big apron on with big pockets, and she would be putting stuff in. Spiderwort it’s called, it gets on a rock, that’s what she was looking for. You never see it anymore. On our land, a lot of it grew in the holler ‘cause there were a lot of rocks there. I never see it anymore.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What’s it called?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Spiderwort.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Spiderwort. Is it good to eat?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It’s delicious to eat when it’s growing. It’s like grass, it had a purple stock below, that’s how you recognized it. To recognize it, it had blue stalks. I’ve seen a lot of mushrooms. I don’t know the different ones, the ones stick on hickory, and the ones they called owls, those big ones. And wishi.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You said owls, is that the ones perched? They will be stuck on there?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah. Have you seen those?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They’re delicious.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, they really were delicious. I was almost grown when I was given something like that. I was asked, “Have you ever eaten something like this?” They said, “You’re gonna eat it now.” And it was good to eat, that.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: We used to look for things like that all the time. They knew just where it grew. And I don’t know that now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Were you driving somewhere then, when you were looking for that?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah. I was little. I could climb just like a monkey.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Do you like onions that live in the woods?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Mixed with eggs.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Poke salad.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about ᎪᏧᏁᎩ they used to call it, have you ever?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I know what it is, but I didn’t like it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That building, they used to get it behind there, ᎪᏧᏁᎩ. I guess it used to grow everywhere.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I’ve forgotten a lot of things that no longer live nowadays. What I’ve seen. ᎬᏂᎩ, they call it, do you know it? Little blackberries. It used to be everywhere in the woods. It’s really delicious to eat. ᎪᎳ ᎬᏍᏗ they used to call it, a lot of round berries. They were very delicious, but I don’t see it anymore.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about what you’re talking about? Did you have to cook them, or what?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: No, you just pick them right there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: The same as huckleberries.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, the same. They look like huckleberries, but they call it ᎪᎳ ᎬᏍᏗ. It was just smaller, but it would be lots of berries.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So you couldn’t find it anymore?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Every now and then, you can find a little bit. And there aren’t any grapes anymore, either. We used to find them everywhere, back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You said grapes, what did y’all make with them?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: We would just eat them right there, just like they do today.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You all would just eat them.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Just like what they have today. Those smaller ones that are just like grapes. What do they call it? Like a grape?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: I don’t know.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Possum grapes. I forgot what they’re called in Cherokee. They made soup from that, it’s delicious. Or they said it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You probably ate a lot of that, too. From the woods?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: From time to time, we would eat that when we went to Grandpa’s. The woods were that way. We would look around when we were at our house. We had that, it wasn’t in the woods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about, us Cherokee we used to look for a lot of things in woods.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It was food then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s probably why we were healthier then, looking for food in the woods.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, me and Richard Pickup were talking, and he was asking me what I’ve eaten in the past and what the names of them were. Cantaloupe, they call it, do you know what that is? Cantaloupe.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh, yeah.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: That’s what they called it and some of them called it ᎪᎰᏍᎦ.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: ᎪᎰᏍᎦ – cantaloupe. Wonder why they named it that, ᎪᎰᏍᎦ.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I don’t know, but that’s what I heard here and there. They called it ᎪᎰᏍᎦ. Richard was fascinated by that. I was telling Richard, and he had never heard that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, me neither, ᎪᎰᏍᎦ. And now ᎬᎩᏍᏗ they called it back then.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: That’s all I know, that they call it watermelon.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now, what about watermelon? Did it grow in the woods then or did someone have to raise it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Someone had to grow it. I’ve never seen it in the woods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was really good when it was cold.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I really liked that. Sometimes it doesn’t agree with my stomach.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: What about water? Where did you all get it from?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: The land that I had at Oak Ridge, I had my own well, and we were getting it out with a bucket and rope.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it round? You would lower it and dip it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Just last summer, first time ever in my life, I found out it had dried up. But people are stuffing things in it when they come around. I just now found out it was drying up. Now, just like that, it was just about that deep [gesture]. The spring never got dry. It’s still there, but it needs to be cleaned. I’m too old to try now.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It never did dry up. The water was always running.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Always.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about your parents? When they were alive, did they do the same thing to get water, or what? Or from a spring?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: When we were little, we lived near about our grandpa’s, how would you say in Cherokee? Spring.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: ᎦᏄᎪᎬ.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: ᎦᏄᎪᎬ. We would go a long ways, and then when we moved, we were dipping it out.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: A well they call it. Well.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: A well. That’s that round thing that’s hanging on a rope. Then when you put it down, it makes a sound when it’s filling up. It was slow, but it was really good to drink back then.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It was really good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was really clean back then.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It was like that on the land on the hill. For two years, I was still getting water to make coffee in the mornings and for cleaning up. It was really clean back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s really good to make coffee with.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: My cousin just lived over there, and was asking me to bring him water. I took him a gallon of water to make coffee with, that dipped out. It was good water.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As for me, I lived around Eucha. They bought it from us, so they could make a lake. And when we moved south of Jay, there was a spring just close by. It was really pretty. There were a lot of Cherokees close by, and they would bring milk.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: ᏚᏄᏐ. They had them in water.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, and cream and a lot of different stuff they would bring. “If you want milk, go ahead and drink, or if you want cream, go ahead and get it.” But we would never do that. Not until they did it themselves. That’s what I’m saying, they watched out for each other real good, the Cherokees.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They watched out for each other a lot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was it like that where you two lived, watching over you all real good?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They would spend the night with each other sometimes and also walk around. One’s name was Tsuliyo Stepp, he lived in Oak Ridge. He would walk to go preach at Salem. He would go Sunday morning and then Sunday evening. He walked seven miles one way. They really believed back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They say, “Let’s have church,” and they really have church. Even if they had to stay all day, they would stay all day.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They used to have church at night, and you don’t hear that anymore.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: They loved each other back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They really helped each other. When they said everybody, everybody showed up.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: When someone got sick, people would gather until midnight, and they would leave on foot down the road.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And they would cook. And they would wash the clothes. Was it the same way?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I wonder where they got their coffee. They drank a lot of it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They were just putting it where the water was, they was just putting it in the water. Were they doing the same?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, they were boiling it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They would be sitting till midnight, drinking their coffee. I guess they were doing the same, right?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: That’s what I try to do, still have gatherings. But I’ve gotten old for them. I don’t go that much.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it was good. We didn’t hardly find money back then, but we made it through.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They used to work in the woods back then.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you two remember when they used to do that, work in the woods? They used to make ties, did y’all do the same?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Oh, yeah, they used to cut locust posts. And what they call white oak, they used to split them. They paid lower for them than locust back then. I used to know all the woods’ names. There’s one kind whose name is hidden from me – cottonwood. I have not heard it in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: mitch-holcomb
segments.translation: Pin Oak, Pin Oak, I think they called it.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Huh-uh, it’s different from Pin Oak. Red Oak, Post Oak. The ones that grow up the creek, they get big. Cottonwood. Someone told me one time what it’s called in Cherokee, but I forgot. I don’t know its name now. I still look around sometimes if somebody somewhere knows. They said it was medicine.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There really were a lot of trees, you said the names of, that were alive and had medicine mixed in them.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, there were a lot, and I know a lot of medicine. I look for it for my family, in the woods, as well as roots. I’ve seen things like that since I was little, and I remember learning. And that’s how long I packed it around on the road. I didn’t tell anyone how much I knew. Do you know what the Mason people are?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What was that?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They call them Masons.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Oh yeah.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I joined that. It was the year ’83 that I joined. Since then, I’ve been involved. They helped people all over the world.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where I’m from, there’s a group like that.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They think they’re secretive. I know if some people know who they are.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? When you were growing up, didn’t you learn things like that? Medicines from the woods?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Huh-uh.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: No, they didn’t tell us things like that.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: They used to tell me a lot. But I didn’t listen. Nowadays, it would have been better if I had listened, I think.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Me too. I look for medicine for a lot of people sometimes. Just certain things. I visit them, and I still find it for them. But it’s hard for me to go far in the woods.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes when you’re in the woods, when you fall, you just fall.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It’s happened to me. Nowadays, I’m still out and about.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: If there’s something he wants to do, he’d be laying there.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I got crippled. When it was raining, I slipped and fell. It crippled me for good. Sometimes I use this [gesture] to help me. It’s been a long time, it’s been about a year, and I’m still in pain.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what happens when you’re getting old. It was easy, but it’s hard to heal and at some point, you don’t heal.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Arthritis. When it gets in you, you can’t heal. How old are you now?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: And me, I did 77 last Saturday. We’re almost the same age, huh?

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We’re almost grown to the same age. I’m thankful for our God that I can still work, that he gave me that.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Really. I finally came to believe. I failed to turn her from her ways. She grew up in church, this one. She tells me I’m hard-headed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Was that true?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Not really. I told her I was just going to join her later on. I told her I couldn’t turn her from her ways.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where do you two go when you two go?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Liberty.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Liberty, now, that’s where you two go?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Just by the house about four to five miles. We’re amongst the white people, Assembly of God.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Now what about what me and you were talking about? As you were growing up, you mentioned your neighbors a while ago.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I stayed with them. It was good for a while, then it got touchy, too. You get suspicious ‘cause you know they’ll get fed up with you, from things that you hear.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You find out.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It’ll bother you at night. They didn’t chase me off, I would just leave. I would realize further down, I would just leave and when I would get somewhere where my cousins live, I would ask them if I could spend the night. They would put me up. “You just stay.” I stayed with my aunts and uncles, and it wasn’t good. It was very lonesome, that feeling would hit me sometimes. Everywhere I wasn’t wanted, you could say. I guess you could say I wasn’t a good boy, I think. I was a little bit of a troublemaker.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: A lot.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: If you ask Charlie Soap, he’ll probably tell you. We were in California one time working on an island. They wouldn’t let us out, they treated us like prisoners. We would cross on a big boat taking us to the island. Once we got there, we couldn’t leave because of the ocean. There was one place with a long bridge in the corner, and you could cross that. One night, they had a guard on the bridge with a gun. They didn’t want you to escape. There were six of us that got together, and I told them, “Let’s go, and I’ll go first.” I realized there was some behind us, but I didn’t know how many there were. Charlie Soap was with them. When we got there, I passed the guard with a gun. He pushed me with it, I grabbed him and threw him in the water. We got away. And Charlie, too, and the others were running behind. We didn’t know we were that close together. Not until I got on the council, and we were talking. He told me what had happened. He said, “I didn’t know who it was that went first, but he threw the first guard in the water.” I told him, “Hey, that was me.”

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? When you were growing up here, what was it like? For instance, looking around and seeing the land y’all were living on? Was it good to live there?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: It was good there for a while. It was just our mom, until she found a man. She just treated certain ones good, and not the rest of us. And when he came, we moved and never came back.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, you all never went back. So, the same thing happened to you, you were lonely?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So, the same thing happened to you, you got a lonesome feeling when you looked around. For instance, the ground wasn’t the same. You got a lonesome feeling when you looked around.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s the way it was. It was good where we lived, and then suddenly it just changed.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like for instance, the scenery suddenly changed, just thinking about it. That’s what will happen, no matter how beautiful your land is. An uncomfortable feeling would come to you, just the way you look around will give you the same feeling.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: It changes the feeling.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, really, and now what about when you two were growing up? Were there Cherokees living there nearby? Were there just Cherokees that were your neighbors when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, when we lived by our grandpa, but when we moved to Short, there were a lot of white people living everywhere. And we were mixed in there.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like you said, too, I guess you went everywhere when you were growing up.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I was coming out everywhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Not just in one place.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Not for long.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: For instance, where you grew up, you weren’t there long.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You weren’t there long.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I was already in Texas when my dad passed away.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you think about, for instance, where you grew up, do you sometimes think where you grew up the first time was good?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: When you were growing up good, does your mind go back there sometimes, where you grew up?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, how I played with others. When I go there sometimes, Janey and Mose still live there. Sometimes, when us two go to Janey’s.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And you two look around. Is that what you two think about, when y’all go there, how good it was when you were growing up?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: It was good, we grew up.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Sometimes you get this lonesome feeling when you go there, and you miss it. “It was this way when I was growing up,” that’s how you’d be thinking, but it all has changed, so I guess you got that kind of feeling.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Everything’s changed nowadays.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Where I grew up there’s houses everywhere.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Where we live, where we bought that land, there wasn’t nobody living there. There was one living there, that Roy Coleman, down that road, but there weren’t any houses. Now they’re all the way around.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We were talking a while ago about food from the woods, and which one do you think is the best?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: To this day, poke salad is my favorite.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Poke salad?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: She likes wild onions.

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: I’ll eat a little bit, but I don’t really like it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about you? Do you like poke salad?

segments.speaker: diane-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, it’s good.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Do you all mix eggs in poke salad? It’s really enjoyable to eat when you do it that way.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: There are a lot of things that are like that if you mix eggs in – if you know how.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Like that one we were talking about early, ᎪᏧᏂ, I don’t like it.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: ᎪᏧᏂ. I never did either. People used to always order it from me, but I didn’t give it to them.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: There isn’t hardly anything like that anymore.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I still believe even nowadays I could recognize that ᏔᏩᎵ. I’m telling you, it was good. I could recognize if I found it somewhere, I think. I don’t know if it’s true. That cottonwood I was telling you about, I’ve been taught a medicine. My hand is shaking – it started just about three months ago. I was told to put that on there, but I can’t find one. I know what it looks like, but I don’t know what it’s called in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Maybe we can look for a name for it in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: No telling. I don’t know what’s wrong with my hand.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: So they said it was medicine for that.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I always look around to see if there’s a tree like that somewhere. I’m gonna get run off for stealing, somewhere.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I was taught, too, but I forget the name of the tree. For instance, you said the roots.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: But this ain’t the roots, it’s the tree. You cut a small piece, and when you cut, there’s a small patch of red underneath the bark. When you get deeper inside the tree, it’s white, and then that has kind of a skin, and that’s good medicine if you have high blood pressure.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: That’s what I was taught. Yeah, that’s what they taught me. And also, for instance, if it’s split, you take that piece and stick it to someone. That’s what I was taught. I was taught that by an elderly lady. Like we said, there were a lot of things back then.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, there was a lot.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Really, God provided that. There were hardly any doctors back then.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Back then when we were coming, it was provided for us but now it’s coming to an end.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s coming to an end. Everyone uses doctors and pills now.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They’re killing us with pills.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: And what about when you talk Cherokee in front of people who don’t speak Cherokee? Are they amazed that you speak Cherokee? Or, where there’s no Cherokees and you meet someone who speaks Cherokee, and there are people standing there who don’t understand Cherokee or who aren’t Cherokee, when you two start talking Cherokee, are they amazed by it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They say they like hearing it. They tell me that it’s beautiful.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: They listen. When us two get to a restaurant and we pray, everyone pays attention. They take their hats off.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Even so much, when you pray in Cherokee?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, if you pray in Cherokee.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, some would say, “It’d be good if I could learn to speak Cherokee.”

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah a lot. There’s one white person I go to church with who really tries. Sometimes it’s aggravating, him asking questions. A little later, he’ll be looking for the same thing. That’s why I couldn’t be a teacher, I was telling him. Muldrow Community Building was calling me to teach Cherokee. I told them no, I wouldn’t do it. Some Sixkiller lady is teaching there, I don’t know her first name.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It’s a woman named Sixkiller.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: She’s teaching there now. I went there the other day. I was interested in what I know and what she was teaching. It’s not the same as what I know, but I don’t say anything.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: What about this? We’re talking Cherokee, and one of these days, someone is going to listen to it. They’re going to say, “That’s the way they used to talk,” when they listen to it. Do you two appreciate the fact that this involves y’all, that they are going to listen to us talking? There’s something they might learn.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: People are trying now, they really want to learn. It might be helpful to them someday, what we believe.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Say, for instance, this Cherokee learning school here, what do y’all think about it?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I’m really happy about it.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, it really is joyful. We really were losing the language for a while and the elders were passing. Good Cherokee speakers. And they knew the names of things in the woods, like cottonwood, you said. They knew the names of them. What about this meeting we had this morning, when we talked? Was it good for y’all? Did y’all like it? Us talking?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, I’m always teaching Cherokee, as well as kin folks, the boys wanna learn. Our grandkids.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: As for me, when we came in here and talked, did y’all like it pretty good?

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Yeah, it was.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: It was good for me, too. I got to know y’all.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: We met again. It’s been 40 years since we’ve seen one another. I thought it was amazing that he recognized me quickly.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Well I appreciated that we was able to talk.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Me too, it might be helpful to someone someday.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: Yeah, that’s what I was saying a minute ago. In time, this conversation will be helpful to someone.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We got to know each other.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: Really.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: I appreciate it, that’s all you can say. Let’s just love one another.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: That’s it, wonder what time it’s getting.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: We’re done now, y’all are probably getting hungry.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I have to go to Tulsa to see a dermatologist, too.

segments.speaker: guy-soldier
segments.translation: You two look after y’allselves.

segments.speaker: sam-daugherty
segments.translation: I appreciate it.
